purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and inspected-source provenance for the six clarity and orientation articles, P01–P06. These fields remain outside the strict Commons frontmatter schema.

articles.title: Move from Familiar to New
use_when: Individual sentences are clear but their progression is hard to follow.
Readers meet a detail before learning the context that makes it useful.
Transition words have not repaired the connection between ideas.
mechanisms: Familiar information as an entry point
not_ideal_when: A brief unfamiliar arrival deliberately creates discovery or curiosity.
A forced chain of repeated words would obscure the paragraph's larger purpose.
example_user_queries: Each sentence makes sense but my paragraph still feels jumpy.
Readers keep looking backward to understand what I mean.
I added transition words and the writing still does not flow.
How can I introduce a new concept without losing people?
The terms in my explanation are familiar to me but not my audience.
My paragraphs feel like separate facts rather than a developing idea.
Do I have to repeat the same subject at the start of every sentence?
I cannot tell how much background to give before a new detail.
How can I keep the connections clear without repeating whole sentences?
Can a story introduce an unfamiliar object before explaining its significance?

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons show the relevant choices and their effects. No separate table or diagram is needed; terms and grammatical relationships are explained where used.

sources.author: Duke Graduate School Scientific Writing Resource
sources.title: Lesson 2: Cohesion, Coherence, and Emphasis
sources.inspected_material: Principle 1 on familiar/new information and Principle 2 on deliberate passive voice, including their explanatory passages.
sources.supports: The craft guidance to connect established information to unfamiliar material and choose sentence order deliberately.
sources.limits: The library notice and narrative alternatives are original. No direct passage-level attribution to Williams or Birkenstein is made, and no measured cognitive benefit is asserted.

articles.title: Put Actors in Subjects and Actions in Verbs
use_when: Actions are buried in abstract nouns while verbs only announce occurrence or requirement.
An account obscures who decided something or who must act next.
A revision exposes a responsibility that has not actually been established.
mechanisms: Aligning grammatical roles with intended actors and actions
not_ideal_when: The actor is unknown or unimportant and should not be invented.
A familiar abstraction or an affected object is the appropriate subject.
example_user_queries: My report describes decisions but nobody can tell who made them.
I use approval and implementation a lot and the prose feels bureaucratic.
Readers do not know who is supposed to act next.
How do I make responsibility clear without blaming someone unfairly?
Should I turn every abstract noun into a verb?
Is passive voice always a problem?
I am trying to sound professional and my sentences have become impersonal.
A rewrite is forcing me to name an actor I do not actually know.
How can I explain several people's roles without making the process confusing?
When is the action itself a useful topic for the next sentence?

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons show the relevant choices and their effects. No separate table or diagram is needed; terms and grammatical relationships are explained where used.

sources.author: Boston University Teaching Writing
sources.title: Sentences Tell Stories: A Principle of Clarity
sources.inspected_material: Conceptual Framework and Part III on nominalizations, including the attribution of the characters/actions formulation to Joseph Williams.
sources.supports: The relationship between grammatical subjects and verbs and the intended characters and actions, with nominalization treated as a possible source of obscurity.
sources.limits: The community-hall example and grammatical alternatives are original. No textbook example or exercise is reproduced, and no complete Williams book passage is claimed to have been checked.

articles.title: Keep Subjects and Verbs Close
use_when: Readers must traverse a long qualification before discovering the main statement.
Background or a long list hides the relation between the subject and its verb.
Moving a qualification risks changing which group or causal relationship the sentence describes.
mechanisms: Making the main statement available earlier
not_ideal_when: A short qualification is essential to identifying the subject.
A deliberate, understandable delay contributes to narrative timing.
example_user_queries: I get lost halfway through my own long sentences.
The main point arrives after a pile of qualifications.
Should I shorten a sentence or move some of its detail?
My editor keeps asking who is doing what even though both are named.
I want to preserve a qualification without burying the action.
Moving a clause seems to change which people my sentence refers to.
Can I keep a long sentence when its rhythm matters?
Is there a rule for how many words can separate a subject from its verb?
Putting all the background first has made my sentence just as hard to follow.
How can a delayed answer create a useful effect in a scene?

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons show the relevant choices and their effects. No separate table or diagram is needed; terms and grammatical relationships are explained where used.

sources.author: Duke Graduate School Scientific Writing Resource
sources.title: Lesson 1: Subjects and Actions
sources.inspected_material: Principle 3 on subject–verb proximity, distinct from Principles 1 and 2 on role selection.
sources.supports: The structural recommendation to reduce burdensome separation between a sentence's subject and verb.
sources.limits: The article does not borrow the source's scientific or list examples and does not assert a fixed distance threshold.

sources.author: Michael Simon, MLA Style Center
sources.title: “Parting Is Such Sweet Sorrow”: When a Comma Separates Subject and Verb
sources.inspected_material: The opening discussion connecting a misplaced comma with excessive subject–verb separation and a possible structural rewrite.
sources.supports: Considering sentence restructuring when the subject and verb have become too far apart.
sources.limits: The tenants' report, restricted-group comparison, and family scene are original. The source is not treated as an empirical study.

articles.title: Make References Unambiguous
use_when: A pronoun or demonstrative has several plausible targets.
Changing labels makes one object or group appear to be several.
A reported opinion is being carried forward as if it were the writer's own judgment.
mechanisms: Naming competing referents where the distinction matters
Maintaining meaningful labels across a passage
Separating uncertainty about identity from uncertainty about significance
not_ideal_when: The referent is already unmistakable and repeated names would burden the prose.
Uncertainty about identity is deliberate and serves a clear literary purpose.
example_user_queries: Readers cannot tell which person I mean by she.
My handover mentions several documents and people keep confusing them.
I know what this refers to but my editor says it is unclear.
How can I avoid repeating names without losing track of who is speaking?
Does changing the noun each time make my writing more elegant?
I want to report someone's criticism without sounding as if I agree.
My sentences are grammatical but readers come away with different accounts of the agreement.
When should I add a noun after this or that?
How can I keep a mystery while making the physical action clear?
A revision would require me to name someone whose role I have not confirmed.

sources.author: Purdue OWL, Purdue University

sources.supports: Checking that readers can identify the intended target of a pronoun and naming it when necessary.
sources.limits: The exhibition update, attributed judgment, and shop scene are original. Stable-label and narrative discussions are editorial synthesis, not attributed textbook passages or empirical claims.

articles.title: Give Each Paragraph a Main Job
use_when: Sentences share a subject but alternate between unfinished lines of thought.
Paragraph breaks reflect visual length rather than a meaningful change.
An example or detail is relevant to the topic but does not develop the paragraph at this point.
mechanisms: Grouping details by the contribution they make
Distinguishing a broad subject from a local purpose
Using breaks to shape changes in thought or experience
not_ideal_when: A rigid topic-sentence formula would flatten dialogue, narrative, or associative prose.
The difficulty concerns missing sections or the order of the whole work rather than local paragraph development.
example_user_queries: All the sentences are about the same thing but my paragraph still wanders.
Where should I put a paragraph break?
My proposal mixes the problem with the arrangements for solving it.
I split a long paragraph and both halves still feel unfinished.
Does every paragraph need a topic sentence?
How do I know whether a detail belongs here or somewhere else?
My paragraphs make claims but never seem to develop them.
Can one paragraph include a claim, an example, and a qualification?
I want paragraph breaks in my story to control the timing.
Do paragraphs have to contain a fixed number of sentences?

sources.author: Harvard College Writing Center
sources.title: Anatomy of a Body Paragraph
sources.inspected_material: The guidance on a main point, topic sentences, evidence, analysis, and paragraph endings; the page explicitly frames these as academic essay guidance.
sources.supports: Developing a local point rather than collecting unsupported statements, and distinguishing evidence from its interpretation.
sources.limits: No source example is reproduced. The repair-café proposal and narrative scene are original; narrative timing is an editorial extension beyond the page's academic-argument scope.

sources.author: UNC Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Paragraphs
sources.inspected_material: The sections What is a paragraph?, How do I decide what to put in a paragraph?, and How do I organize a paragraph?, including the distinction between unity and length and the list of development forms.
sources.supports: Paragraph unity is not a fixed sentence count, and paragraph organization depends on the purpose of the development.
sources.limits: No five-step formula or source illustration is reproduced or prescribed across genres. Fiction and associative-prose discussion is editorial synthesis.

articles.title: Signal the Real Relationship
use_when: Readers understand individual statements but cannot tell why one follows another.
A transition implies causation or a settled conclusion that the evidence does not support.
A qualification is mistaken for opposition because the particular connection is unstated.
mechanisms: Identifying the relation before choosing a transition
Explaining the specific connection when a broad connector leaves it uncertain
Using clause structure to assign emphasis
not_ideal_when: The relationship is already available and extra signposting would interrupt the prose.
The argument lacks evidence or a supporting reason that no connector can provide.
example_user_queries: My essay feels like separate statements even though each sentence makes sense.
I keep adding however and therefore but the argument still feels weak.
Am I claiming cause and effect when I only know what happened first?
Readers think I oppose a proposal when I only question its deadline.
How do I show that the next point qualifies the first one?
Do I need a transition at the start of every paragraph?
A conclusion sounds convincing but I cannot explain why it follows.
How can sentence structure change which idea gets the emphasis?
My editor says the connection between these paragraphs is missing.
Explaining the contrast in my story seems to spoil the effect.

sources.author: Harvard College Writing Center
sources.title: Transitions
sources.inspected_material: The discussion of identifying relationships before choosing transitional words, the comparison/concession/elaboration categories, and the caution about accurate causal links.
sources.supports: Choosing signals to fit an established relationship rather than adding connectors as decoration or using causal terms without a supported connection.
sources.limits: The arts-centre figures, magazine proposal, and café scene are original hypothetical examples. Sentence emphasis and narrative implication are editorial synthesis; no empirical or book-passage claim is made.
